keckle.c: KECKLE; when the Cables of a Ship gaul in the Hawse, or the Bolt-ropes do so against the Ship's Quarter, the Seamen wind some small Ropes about them; and this serving of these Ropes is called Keck ling. -

kedging.c: KEDGING, at Sea, is when a Ship is brought up or down in a narrow River, the Wind being contrary to the Tide, and yet she into go with the ide; then they use to fet their Fore-fail, or Fore - fail and the Missen, and so let the Ship drive with the Tide, that so they may flat her about; and if she happen to come over too near the Shoar, they have a final Anchor in the Head of their Boat with a Hawser fastened to it from the Ship, which Anchor they then let fall in the Middle of the Stream, and so wind or turn her Head about, lifting the Anchor up again when she is come fully about: This Work is called Kedging, or to kedge up a River, and the Anchor made ule of is called the

keel.c: KEEL, is the lowest Piece of Timber in a Ship, in the Bottom of her Hull; one End whereof is at the Term, the other at the Stem: Into this are all the Ground-Timbers and Hooks fastened, and bolted fore and aft. When a Ship hath a deep Keel, she is said to have a Rank Keel; and this serves well to keep her from rowling; but if the is overfloat and rowls too much, a new Keel is sometimes put on, called a False Keel.

keelrope.c: KEEL-ROPE, a Hair-Rope running between the rk and the Keel of a Ship, to clear and gt soles when they are choaked up with Ba - alt, s'c.

keelson.c: KEELSON, the next Piece of Timber in a Ship to her Keel, lying right over it next above the Floor-Timber.

keeperofthegreatseal.c: KEEPER of the Great Seal, is a Lord by his Office, and stile Lord-Keeper of the Great Seal of England: He is one of the King's Privy-Council; through whose Hands pass all Charters, Commissions, and Grants of the King under the Great Seal 5 without which Sea / all such Instruments by Law are of no force: For the King is, in the Interpretation of Law, a Corporation, and passeth nothing firmly but under the said Seal, which is as the publick Faith of the Kingdom, in the high Esteem and Reputation justly attributed thereto. This Lord-Keeper hath the same Place, Authority, Preheminence, JurifdiGion, Execution of Laws, and all other Customs, Commodities, and Advantages, as the Lord-Chancellor of England hath for the Time being. He is constituted by the Delivery of the Great Seal to him, and taking his Oath.

keeperoftheprivyseal.c: KEEPER of the Privy Seal, is a Lord by his Office, through whose Hands pass all Charters signed by the King, before they come to the great Seal, and some things which do not pass the Great Seal at all. He is of the King's Privy Council, and one of the Great Officers of the King - om.

kidneys.c: KIDNEYS. The Kidneys in Man are always two in Number, one n each Side, being nearly of the Figure of the French ot Kidney - Beans; which latter Name they take from being like the Kidneys.,. k; The Length of the human Kidney is between four and five Fingert Breadth: They ate about two Fingers. Breadth in Thickness, and three over. The ree Kidney is situated under the Liver; the left under the Spleen. In a Feetus their external Substance is divided into several Lobes join d tngetber which in adult Persons become more c pxebedeenie such their Surface is equal and. have two Membranes; one Common from the Peritoneum, the other Proper, Usually they are co - ver'd with 5 gee deal of Fat; their Colour is of a dark Ri f There are several Lymphatic Less ls observed in the Kidneys, which discharge themselves. into Pecquet's Repository: The Veins go into the Vena Cava: The Arteries come from the " orta, Those Veins and Arteries are called Emulents: They come out from the Kidneys in their follow Sides ( which lie nearest to the Cava and Aorta) included in one common pfula, and are divided into several Branches, which surround the Pelvis, These Branches are again fub-divided into an Infinity of other lesser ones, which go to the external Parts of the Kidneys, where they inosculate, and form a kind of Ne; from which their Extremities coming, terminate al - so in Infinity of Glands, which are all very small. These Glands are in Figure roundish, and they compose the outer Substance of the Kidneys; which is half a Finger thick. From ach of them there along mall Tube; and the Collect tion of these Tubes compose the innermost Substance of the Kidneys. As these Ti bules approach the Pelvis; they gather together in little Bundles; whose Extremities piercing the Membrane of the Pelvis, form those little Protuberances on the Inside of the Pelvis, or Cavity in the middle of the Kidney, which are called the Papille. g This Cavity; or Pelvis, is'form d by the Dila tation of the Uve ters: It fends out several Ramifications, which divide the Urinary Tubes into Bundles, and which make a sort of Cupjula to the Blood Vessels. The Use of the Kidneys is to separate the Urine from the Blood; which by the Motion of the Heart and Arteries is thrust into the Emulgent Branches, which catty it to the little lands; by whose Means the Serosity being fe - poet is received by the Orifice of the little ubes, which go from those Glands to the Pelvis; from whence it runs by the Ureters into the Bladder. The Blood which was carried into the Glands, its Particles bar 3 too gross to enter into the mall excretory Tubes, is brought back from the Kidneys by the Emulgent Veins, to be mingled with the other Venal Blood in the Cava. The Description of the Ureters, Vesica Urinaria, Glandule Renales, 7 c, you will find in their proper Places.: Dr. Keil, in his Animal Secretion, pag. 33 judges that the Kidneys are placed so near the art as they are, because Salts are Corpuscles; which are strongly attracted, and have a most close Union with the Fluid of Water: For tho the Lungs may divide the Particles of Salt one from another, yet still they firmly adhere to the aqueous Humour in which they swim 5 the they may likewise at first be drawn off: And he thinks that che Kidney: could not well have been ge ata greater Distance, to have separated such a Quantity of Urine as they flow do; and thar-not only on the account of the Quantities of Blood they receive where they are; but likewise, if they had a more distant Situation; other Particles must have united with the Salts and aqueous Particles ( as even in their present Station some terrestrial Particles do) and nips A the Urine could not have been distilled such as it is now, or at least burin a small Quantity.

kingdomaterm.c: KINGDOM, a Term used by the Chymifts, who, according to their Cant in other things, call the Three Orders of Natural Bodies, Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral, by the Name of Kingdom. Thus they would fay, Those Bodies which belong to the Animal Kingdom, abound most in Volatile Salt..: 4

kingsbench.c: KING'S-BENCH, is the Court or Judgment - Seat, where the King of England was sometimes wont to fit in his own Person; and therefore it was moveable with the Court or King's Houfhold, and called Curia Domini Regis, and Aula Regia, as Gwin reports in his Preface to bis Reading, and that therein, and in the Court of Exchequer, which were the only Courts of the King till Heary the Third's Days, were handled all Matters of Justice, as well Civil as Criminal. This Court of the King's-Bench, was wont in Ancient Times to be especially exercised in all Criminal Matters and Pleas of the Crown, Jeaving the handling of private Contra ts and Civil A ions to the Common-Pleas, and other Courts.

knaveline.c: KNAVE-LINE, is a Rope in a Ship, fastened to the Cross-Trees under the Main or Fore-Top, whence it comes down by the Ties to the Ram head, and there tis reeved through a Piece of Wood of about two Foot long, and so is brought to the Pye dy Side, and there haled up taught to the ails. Its Use is to keep the Ties and Halliards from turning about one another, as they are apt to do when new and first used; and therefore after the are a little used and stretched, this Knave-Line is taken away, of no further Ute.
